title: Backup, Recovery & Ops
summary: Running a database in production means more than queries — it means not losing data, recovering fast, and knowing what's breaking before users do.

blocks.markdown:
Production databases need more than correct queries — they need **durability** (you never lose committed data), **availability** (the DB stays up), and **observability** (you know when something is wrong).

- **Backup** — copies of data taken periodically.
- **Recovery** — restoring data after a failure.
- **RPO / RTO** — how much data loss and how much downtime you can tolerate.
- **High availability** — keeping the DB reachable despite failures.
- **ORM** — app-layer bridge to the DB, with its own pitfalls.

blocks.subTitle: Full backup
blocks.markdown:
A **full backup** copies every byte of the database at a point in time.

- **Pros:** self-contained — restore from a single file; simple.
- **Cons:** large and slow — copying the whole DB every time is expensive.

Typical cadence: weekly full backup as the baseline, supplemented by incremental or differential backups in between.

blocks.subTitle: Incremental vs differential
blocks.markdown:
**Incremental backup** — copies only blocks changed since the **last backup** (full or incremental).

**Differential backup** — copies everything changed since the **last full backup**.

- Incremental: smallest backups, but restore needs the full + every incremental in chain.
- Differential: larger than incremental but restore only needs full + one differential.

Pick differential when fast restore matters; pick incremental when storage cost matters.

blocks.subTitle: Comparison
blocks.markdown:
At a glance:

| Type | What it copies | Restore needs |
|---|---|---|
| Full | Everything | Full only |
| Differential | Since last full | Full + 1 diff |
| Incremental | Since last backup | Full + all increments |

Smaller backup → more pieces to stitch at restore time.

**Point-in-time recovery (PITR)** lets you restore a database to any moment in the past — not just to your last backup.

How it works: the DB continuously writes a **WAL (write-ahead log)** — every change logged before it is applied. To recover:
1. Restore the last full backup.
2. **Replay WAL logs** up to the target timestamp.

Example: a bad migration runs at 14:05 — restore the backup and replay logs up to 14:04. See [transaction-management-concurrency](transaction-management-concurrency) for WAL internals.

Two metrics define your recovery goals:

- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** — the maximum age of data you can afford to lose. If your RPO is 1 hour, you must back up at least every hour.
- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** — the maximum downtime you can afford. If your RTO is 15 minutes, the DB must be back up within 15 minutes of a failure.

Lower RPO and RTO cost more — continuous WAL shipping, hot standbys, faster hardware.

blocks.subTitle: Comparison
blocks.markdown:
RPO vs RTO side by side:

| Metric | Measures | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| RPO | Data loss tolerance | How old can the restored data be? |
| RTO | Downtime tolerance | How fast must the DB be back? |

Both are set by business requirements, then the architecture is designed to meet them.

**High availability (HA)** means the DB keeps serving requests even when one node fails.

- **Standby replica** — a copy of the primary, kept in sync. Two kinds:
  - **Hot standby** — ready to take traffic immediately.
  - **Warm standby** — synced, but needs a moment to start serving.
- **Failover** — the process of promoting a standby to primary when the primary dies. Can be automatic (managed by a cluster manager like Patroni) or manual.

See [sharding-replication-scaling](sharding-replication-scaling) for replication mechanics.

**Disaster recovery (DR)** plans for catastrophic failures — datacenter fire, cloud region outage — where your primary and its standbys are all gone.

- Maintain a **DR replica in a separate region or cloud zone**.
- DR replicas typically lag more than local standbys (higher RPO).
- Test the DR plan regularly — a backup you've never restored is a backup you don't trust.
- **3-2-1 rule:** 3 copies, on 2 different media, with 1 offsite.

You can't fix what you don't see. Key DB metrics to watch:

- **Active connections** — approaching the connection limit means app threads will start hanging.
- **Slow queries** — queries above a threshold (logged via `slow_query_log` in MySQL, `log_min_duration_statement` in Postgres).
- **Replication lag** — how far behind is a replica? High lag means stale reads and a larger gap to recover.
- **Disk usage** — WAL and data files grow; run out of disk and the DB halts.
- **Lock waits** — long-running locks block writers and signal transaction trouble.

An **ORM (Object-Relational Mapper)** lets app code talk to a relational DB using objects instead of SQL.

- Map a class `User` to the `users` table; calling `user.save()` generates the INSERT.
- Popular ORMs: ActiveRecord (Ruby/Rails), SQLAlchemy (Python), Hibernate (Java), Prisma (Node).
- **Leaky abstraction** — the ORM hides SQL, but bad queries still hurt. You must understand the SQL it generates.

See [query-optimization-indexes](query-optimization-indexes) for query-level tuning.

blocks.subTitle: The N+1 problem
blocks.markdown:
The **N+1 problem** is the most common ORM pitfall: fetching a list of N records, then issuing a separate query for each one's association.

Example: load 100 posts, then for each post load its author — that's 1 + 100 = 101 queries instead of 1 join.

Fix: **eager loading** — tell the ORM to join the association upfront (`.includes(:author)` in ActiveRecord, `.joinedload()` in SQLAlchemy). See [caching-performance](caching-performance) for further query cost reduction.

blocks.subTitle: Migrations
blocks.markdown:
**Migrations** are versioned, incremental scripts that change the database schema — add a column, create an index, drop a table.

- Stored in version control alongside code so schema changes are reproducible.
- Must be **backward compatible** in production: add columns nullable first, backfill, then add constraints — never drop a column the old code still reads.
- A bad migration on a large table can lock it for minutes; PITR is your safety net.

blocks.subTitle: Backup types
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What are full, incremental, and differential backups?**

**Full** copies everything; slow and large but simplest to restore. **Incremental** copies only what changed since the last backup — smallest files, slowest restore (must replay every increment). **Differential** copies everything since the last full — larger than incremental but restores in two steps (full + one diff). Choose by your RTO budget.

blocks.subTitle: RPO and RTO
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What are RPO and RTO?**

**RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** is the maximum data loss you can accept — it sets how often you must back up. **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** is the maximum downtime you can accept — it sets how fast you must recover. Example: RPO = 1 hour means you back up every hour; RTO = 15 min means you need a hot standby, not a cold restore.

blocks.subTitle: PITR and N+1
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is point-in-time recovery?**

Restore a backup and then replay WAL (write-ahead log) entries up to the exact minute you want — so you can undo a bad migration without losing all subsequent data.

⭐ **Q: What is the N+1 problem with ORMs?**

Fetching a list of N rows then issuing N separate queries for each row's association — 101 queries instead of 1 join. Fix with eager loading so the ORM fetches associations in one pass.
